ACT-RD7-P1-Q1.pick: the booming face is a dry, loosely packed layer lying over a denser, damper bed.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q1.note: Para 2 names the geophones and then 'the result that organized everything else': the face is layered. D is the best trap - 90 Hz is a real number in the passage but it is reported from the crest in para 1, before any instrument exists, so the stem's 'geophone measurements were what established' excludes it. C is refuted by 'lasts as long as the avalanche does'. Fidelity: no line cite; the quoted-in-explanation spans all match the passage as shipped. Subject recall: could NOT have answered from general knowledge - the instrument and its depths are passage-specific.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q2.pick: a decrease in the thickness of the dry surface layer.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q2.note: 'fifty-one centimetres thick in October and twenty-nine in March; the dominant frequency rose from 76 hertz to 104' plus the stated rule that layer thickness 'selects which frequencies survive'. A is the best distractor in the set: it is Passage B's rival account of the SAME numbers, so anyone reading the pair as one text picks it. C is denied outright ('The grains were the same grains'); D is never measured. Exclusive because the stem is attribution-keyed to Passage A. Fidelity: the 76/104 figures in the stem match the passage exactly. Subject recall: YES, partially - the waveguide camp's real-world claim is that layer thickness sets the note, so a physics-literate solver can pick B from priors without reading. Recall and text agree here, so it costs measurement, not accuracy.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q3.pick: a grain striking early is slowed and a grain striking late is driven forward.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q3.note: Verbatim restatement of Passage B para 2. B (steel floor reflecting energy) is the only distractor with any pull, because it imports Passage A's reflection language into Passage B's apparatus - a nice cross-passage trap, but the floor is mentioned only as what the sand is poured onto. C is explicitly ruled out ('no damp bed under a dry layer'); D invents a sorting mechanism. Subject recall: YES, partially - the collective-collision / synchronization mechanism is the published position of the shear-rate camp, and option A restates it; answerable from priors.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q4.pick: booming does not require the layered structure that Passage A describes.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q4.note: The chute paragraph is built as a subtraction - no dune, no seasons, no damp bed under a dry layer - and it booms anyway at 95 Hz. D is the sharpest distractor because 'two metres long' invites a scale objection, but Passage B offers the chute as sufficient, not as a limitation, so D inverts its stance. A (loudness) and B (unusual sand) are unsupported - B is actively contradicted by 'with nobody tuning anything'. Subject recall: YES, partially - that lab chutes reproduce booming without a dune is a known result; C is reachable from priors alone.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q5.pick: A thinner dry layer avalanches faster, so the shear rate changed as well.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q5.note: Best item in the paired set. The stem asks what the ambiguity CHARGE depends on, and the answer is the confound Passage B supplies: 'the crust ... weakens as the sand dries, and a thinner dry layer avalanches faster'. A is the strongest wrong option and it is wrong for a precise reason - 'The grains were the same grains' is the part both sides agree on, so it cannot be what makes the result cut two ways; a solver who grabs it has confused a shared premise with a disputed one. B and D are objections Passage B never raises. Fidelity: option C reproduces the passage clause exactly. Subject recall: NO - this is a reasoning-about-confounds item with no real-world answer to recall.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q6.pick: allowing no excuse if it turns out to be wrong.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q6.note: 'unforgiving' is attached to the PREDICTION, not to the researchers or the fieldwork, and the sentence that follows states the prediction in pass/fail form ('the note must move when the layer does') and cites publishing the profiles alongside the recordings. B is the only distractor worth anything - trenching a dune face twice is laborious - but the adjective's head noun settles it. A reads the word as manner toward opponents; C is about reception, which the passage never touches. Fidelity: 'unforgiving' appears once, in Passage A para 3, as the stem says. Subject recall: NO - vocabulary in context.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q7.pick: accepting the measurement but denying that it separates the two accounts.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q7.note: 'we do not think it is a mistake. We think it is ambiguous' plus 'The field result agrees with both accounts' gives both halves. The option set is well built because it varies along exactly the two axes that matter - accept/reject, and what the acceptance implies - so each wrong option is a specific misreading rather than noise. C is the trap for a solver who registers only 'we take it seriously'; D for one who assumes a rival must reject the data. Subject recall: NO - this is about what Passage B DOES, not about dunes.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q8.pick: it grants that without an avalanche there is no energy to guide.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q8.note: Passage A para 4 is the pre-emption: 'We do not say the avalanche is unimportant. Without one there is no energy to guide', then it divides the labour. The item is hard mainly because it requires holding Passage B's objection in mind while scanning A for a concession. The three wrong options are all concessions Passage A never makes, and C is the best of them because February IS a limit case - but the passage explains it ('after rain') rather than conceding it is unexplained. A misreads a method statement as a regret. Fidelity: option D matches 'Without one there is no energy to guide' with only the pronoun expanded. Subject recall: NO.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q9.pick: Sound is produced only while an avalanche is in motion.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q9.note: Exclusive because no second option survives: B is refuted by A booming at both 51 cm and 29 cm, C by B's own range-covering formula, D by B's steel floor with no damp bed. But FLAGGING the key as strained, and this is the item I would send to the human sitting first. Passage B's whole opening exists to show booming with NO dune and no avalanche - eight centimetres of poured sand sheared in a chute. So Passage B would endorse 'only while the layer is being sheared', and 'avalanche' is the author's gloss for shear, not Passage B's word. A careful solver can reach the key only by treating avalanche and shear as interchangeable, which Passage B spends a paragraph separating. The failure mode is a solver rejecting all four rather than choosing a rival - which on a four-choice item shows up as noise, not as a split. Recommend rewording the key to 'only while the sand is in motion' or 'only while the layer is shearing'; that costs nothing and removes the one term Passage B has disclaimed. The explanation's parenthetical ('shearing the layer, which is what an avalanche does') concedes the same gap. Subject recall: NO.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q1.pick: whose ordinary effort the standard is measured against.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q1.note: 'The rulebook says ordinary effort. It does not say whose ordinary.' D is a direct unpacking. A is the strongest distractor and is cleanly excluded by the paragraph immediately above, which partitions authority (balls, strikes, outs to the umpire; hit-or-error to the scorer). B mistakes the question the standard exists to answer for the gap IN the standard - a genuine and useful confusion. C invents an unseen play; she is in the press box watching. Fidelity: stem paraphrases rather than quotes; 'ordinary effort' appears as shipped in para 2.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q2.pick: an account of how things already stand.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q2.note: The word is defined by its contrast partner one sentence earlier: 'He meant it as instruction. I took it as description, which is how a person mistakes a wish for a fact.' Instruction is the ought, description is the is, and 'wish for a fact' confirms it. A is a strong distractor precisely because it is the correct gloss of the OTHER term in the pair - a solver who loses track of which way the sentence runs picks it. D ('a category into which a thing is sorted') is a real dictionary sense of description and is the second-best trap. Author labelled this easy; I would call it medium - the abstract is/ought contrast is harder than a typical ACT vocabulary item. Fidelity: CHECKED - the stem cites 'paragraph 3', and paragraph [3] as shipped is indeed the father's-saying paragraph containing 'description'. Correct.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q3.pick: reached a judgment on the play and knew it was not theirs to enter.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q3.note: 'Four hundred people ruled on the play in the same half second and then remembered that the ruling was not theirs' supplies both halves of A verbatim. B is the closest call in the literary passage and deserves a note: 'not a groan and not a cheer' is, on its own, consistent with a divided crowd, and the text does NOT actually say the four hundred agreed - only that they all ruled at the same instant. So the published explanation's line 'The crowd is unanimous in that half second' is an overclaim and should be softened; it is not what makes B wrong. What makes B wrong is that the very next clause supplies the passage's own account of that sound (they remembered the ruling was not theirs), and 'most strongly indicates' asks for the supported reading, not the merely available one. Exclusive stands, but this is the item I would watch if the sitting shows a split.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q4.pick: supply the standard against which she later measures her own ruling.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q4.note: The saying returns at the two load-bearing moments - 'my father would have said reaching is not catching' inside the ruling, and 'true in a way he did not intend' in the close - so paragraph 3 functions as the yardstick. B is the good distractor: the father's standard IS turned against her, but by her, not by him; he never rules on the play and is not present. D fails on the detail it leans on - ruled index cards versus the league's bound book in a canvas bag is a change, not a continuity. A is unsupported.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q5.pick: was managing her awareness of an outcome she preferred.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q5.note: She names who is in the window, then says 'not looking up was itself a decision, and that I made it very deliberately, which is not what a person does who wants nothing' - and para 8 states the preference outright. Author labelled hard; the trailing clause is a strong enough signpost that I would call it medium. A is refuted by the whole park having gone quiet; C invents an anticipated objection; D is defeated by 'The pencil had already written something' - there is no clerical act left to concentrate on. Fidelity: CHECKED - the quoted span 'did not look up at the press-box window' matches para 6 as shipped word for word.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q6.pick: It entered as a failure a play that few shortstops would have reached.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q6.note: 'She had reached a ball that ninety shortstops in a hundred do not reach, and the book said that she had failed.' C is an excellent distractor and turns on a real detail a fast reader will miss: the paper ran 'the line score with a 0 under H and a 1 under E' - a line score carries no player names, so her name was never printed under the error. B and D both extend past the text's horizon (the narrator gives the bag back in August and says nothing about the next season; Marguerite is never given a view of the rulebook). Author labelled medium; agreed.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q7.pick: acceptance of it on grounds he did not intend.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q7.note: 'my father's saying is true in a way he did not intend' gives both halves - kept, and re-grounded. A is the strong distractor because the item hinges on a single qualifier; a solver who reads only 'is true' picks it. C is excluded by her keeping the rule, D by 'perhaps four hundred times' before the game. Exclusive: A is not defensible once the qualifier is read, and it is read on any careful pass.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q8.pick: is recalling, long afterward, an episode she has not settled for herself.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q8.note: Retrospective markers are dense ('I used to find comforting', 'I have thought since', 'I no longer think') and the close is explicitly unresolved: 'I have never been sure whether that is why I wrote what I wrote.' C is the only distractor with a hook - people in the IGA told her she got it right - but she reports not arguing with them, which the passage frames as her pattern of silence, not endorsement (she also does not argue with Marguerite's silence). A and B are ruled out by the retrospection and by her being the one holding the pencil. Author labelled hard; I would call it medium - the two markers do most of the work.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q9.pick: turn the book from a record into an opinion that has to be weighed.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q9.note: Near-verbatim: 'the book stops being a record and becomes an opinion with her name on it, and everyone who reads it, herself included, has to weigh it.' A is the best distractor because consistency is the reason one would EXPECT for this rule, and the passage pointedly does not give it - her worry is about what the artifact becomes, not about her own steadiness. C (appeals) and D (staffing) appear nowhere. Author labelled hard; the answer sits in one clause of the cited paragraph, so medium.
